title: 1 Kings 20:31–43
context: Ben Hadad’s servants appeal to Ahab’s mercy, and Ahab spares him and makes a treaty. A prophet then uses an enacted parable to bring Ahab to condemn himself for releasing the man the LORD had devoted to destruction.

verses.text: His servants said to him, “See now, we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful kings. Please let us put sackcloth on our bodies and ropes on our heads, and go out to the king of Israel. Maybe he will save your life.”
verses.arminianNotes: His servants say, “we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful kings,” and suggest sackcloth and ropes. Arminian readers see desperate hope placed in Israel’s reputation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the servants seeking mercy. The text does not explain what lay behind that reputation, and readers in this tradition avoid speculating about it.

verses.text: So they put sackcloth on their bodies and ropes on their heads, and came to the king of Israel, and said, “Your servant Ben Hadad says, ‘Please let me live.’ ” He said, “Is he still alive? He is my brother.”
verses.arminianNotes: They come in sackcloth and say, “Your servant Ben Hadad says, ‘Please let me live.’” Ahab replies, “Is he still alive? He is my brother.” Arminian readers see Ahab responding warmly to a defeated enemy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note Ahab’s surprising language. Many in this tradition see “brother” as the language of royal treaty rather than personal affection, though the text does not explain it.

verses.text: Now the men observed diligently and hurried to take this phrase; and they said, “Your brother Ben Hadad.” Then he said, “Go, bring him.” Then Ben Hadad came out to him; and he caused him to come up into the chariot.
verses.arminianNotes: The men quickly seize the phrase: “Your brother Ben Hadad.” Ahab brings him into his chariot. Arminian readers see Ahab moving swiftly toward reconciliation without seeking the LORD’s direction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Ahab acting on his own judgment. The narrative presents the events as they happened and lets the coming prophetic rebuke supply the evaluation.

verses.text: Ben Hadad said to him, “The cities which my father took from your father I will restore. You shall make streets for yourself in Damascus, as my father made in Samaria.” “I”, said Ahab, “will let you go with this covenant.” So he made a covenant with him and let him go.
verses.arminianNotes: Ben Hadad promises to restore cities, and Ahab answers that he “will let you go with this covenant.” Arminian readers see a political bargain that Ahab chose instead of carrying out God’s purpose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Ahab making a treaty on his own terms. Readers in this tradition note that the narrator does not comment here, leaving the verdict to the prophet in verse 42.

verses.text: A certain man of the sons of the prophets said to his fellow by the LORD’s word, “Please strike me!” The man refused to strike him.
verses.arminianNotes: A man of the sons of the prophets says to his fellow “by the LORD’s word, ‘Please strike me!’” but the man refuses. Arminian readers see a strange command testing obedience to God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the scene as a prophetic sign leading to judgment. Readers in both traditions commonly treat this unusual episode as shared ground about the seriousness of obeying God’s word.

verses.text: Then he said to him, “Because you have not obeyed the LORD’s voice, behold, as soon as you have departed from me, a lion will kill you.” As soon as he had departed from him, a lion found him and killed him.
verses.arminianNotes: He says, “Because you have not obeyed the LORD’s voice … a lion will kill you,” and it happens. Arminian readers see a sobering account of disobedience to a clear word from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a severe judgment recorded without softening. The scene recalls 1 Kings 13:24, and readers in this tradition generally treat it as underscoring the authority of God’s word rather than a general pattern.

verses.text: Then he found another man, and said, “Please strike me.” The man struck him and wounded him.
verses.arminianNotes: He finds another man who strikes and wounds him. Arminian readers see obedience to the prophetic instruction, setting up the enacted parable that follows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the wound preparing the sign for Ahab. The contrast with the previous man highlights the difference between refusing and obeying God’s word.

verses.text: So the prophet departed and waited for the king by the way, and disguised himself with his headband over his eyes.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet waits for the king, disguised with a headband over his eyes. Arminian readers see a prophetic sign designed to lead Ahab to judge himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a carefully staged parable. The disguise recalls other prophetic confrontations where a story exposes the king’s own guilt.

verses.text: As the king passed by, he cried to the king, and he said, “Your servant went out into the middle of the battle; and behold, a man came over and brought a man to me, and said, ‘Guard this man! If by any means he is missing, then your life shall be for his life, or else you shall pay a talent of silver.’
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet tells of guarding a captive on pain of “your life shall be for his life, or else you shall pay a talent of silver.” Arminian readers see a story that mirrors Ahab’s own responsibility for Ben Hadad.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a parable drawing Ahab into a verdict. The engwebp footnote explains a talent as a weight of about 30 kilograms; it is a measurement note, not a variant.

verses.text: As your servant was busy here and there, he was gone.” The king of Israel said to him, “So shall your judgment be. You yourself have decided it.”
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet says the captive was gone, and Ahab answers, “So shall your judgment be. You yourself have decided it.” Arminian readers see Ahab unknowingly pronouncing his own sentence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the parable succeed. Ahab’s quick judgment on another exposes his failure in the very matter he has just handled.

verses.text: He hurried, and took the headband away from his eyes; and the king of Israel recognized that he was one of the prophets.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet removes the headband, and the king recognizes him as one of the prophets. Arminian readers see the moment of revelation when the parable’s meaning becomes clear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the disguise give way to confrontation. The recognition prepares for the direct word of judgment that follows.

verses.text: He said to him, “The LORD says, ‘Because you have let go out of your hand the man whom I had devoted to destruction, therefore your life will take the place of his life, and your people take the place of his people.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD says, ‘Because you have let go out of your hand the man whom I had devoted to destruction, therefore your life will take the place of his life.’” Arminian readers see judgment for incomplete obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Ahab judged for releasing the one God had devoted. Readers in both traditions commonly compare 1 Samuel 15 and treat this as shared ground on the seriousness of partial obedience.

verses.text: The king of Israel went to his house sullen and angry, and came to Samaria.
verses.arminianNotes: The king goes home “sullen and angry.” Arminian readers see Ahab reacting with resentment rather than repentance to the prophetic word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a hardened response. The same phrase returns in 21:4, linking this episode with Ahab’s reaction to Naboth’s refusal.
